entries.content_plain: CHAPTER 4 Php 4:1-23 . Exhortations: Thanks for the Supply from Philippi: Greeting; and Closing Benediction. 1. "Wherefore"; since we have such a glorious hope ( Php 3:20 , 21 ). dearly beloved-- repeated again at the close of the verse, implying that his great love to them should be a motive to their obedience. longed for-- "yearned after" in your absence ( Php 1:8 ). crown-- in the day of the Lord ( Php 2:16 ; 1Th 2:19 ). so-- as I have admonished you. stand fast-- ( Php 1:27 ).

And--</hi>Greek, "Yea."<div eID="gen36122" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36123" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">true yoke-fellow--</hi>yoked with me in the same Gospel yoke (<reference osisRef="Matt.11.29">Mt 11:29</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.11.30">30</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.17">1Ti 5:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.18">18</reference>). Either Timothy, Silas (<reference osisRef="Acts.15.40">Ac 15:40</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.16.19">16:19</reference>, at Philippi), or the chief bishop of Philippi. Or else the Greek, "Sunzugus," or "Synzygus," is a proper name: "Who art truly, as thy name means, a yoke-fellow." Certainly not Paul's wife, as <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.5">1Co 9:5</reference> implies he had none.<div eID="gen36123" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36124" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">help those women--</hi>rather, as Greek, "help them," namely, Euodia and Syntyche. "Co-operate with them" [Birks]; or as Alford, "Help in the work of their reconciliation."<div eID="gen36124" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36125" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which laboured with me--</hi>"inasmuch as they labored with me." At Philippi, women were the first hearers of the Gospel, and Lydia the first convert. It is a coincidence which marks genuineness, that in this Epistle alone, special instructions are given to women who labored with Paul in the Gospel. In selecting the first teachers, those first converted would naturally be fixed on. Euodia and Syntyche were doubtless two of "the women who resorted to the riverside, where prayer was wont to be made" (<reference osisRef="Acts.16.13">Ac 16:13</reference>), and being early converted, would naturally take an active part in teaching other women called at a later period; of course not in public preaching, but in a less prominent sphere (<reference osisRef="1Tim.2.11">1Ti 2:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.12">12</reference>).<div eID="gen36125" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36126" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Clement--</hi>bishop of Rome shortly after the death of Peter and Paul. His Epistle from the Church of Rome to the Church of Corinth is extant. It makes no mention of the supremacy of the See of Peter. He was the most eminent of the apostolical fathers. Alford thinks that the Clement here was a Philippian, and not necessarily Clement, bishop of Rome. But Origen [Commentary, John 1:29] identifies the Clement here with the bishop of Rome.<div eID="gen36126" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36127" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the book of life--</hi>the register-book of those whose "citizenship is in heaven" (<reference osisRef="Luke.10.20">Lu 10:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.3.20">Php 3:20</reference>). Anciently, free cities had a roll book containing the names of all those having the right of citizenship (compare <reference osisRef="Exod.32.32">Ex 32:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.69.28">Psa 69:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.13.9">Eze 13:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.12.1">Da 12:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.20.12">Re 20:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.21.27">21:27</reference>). <div eID="gen36127" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 3. And-- Greek, "Yea." true yoke-fellow-- yoked with me in the same Gospel yoke ( Mt 11:29 , 30 ; compare 1Ti 5:17 , 18 ). Either Timothy, Silas ( Ac 15:40 ; 16:19 , at Philippi), or the chief bishop of Philippi. Or else the Greek, "Sunzugus," or "Synzygus," is a proper name: "Who art truly, as thy name means, a yoke-fellow." Certainly not Paul's wife, as 1Co 9:5 implies he had none. help those women-- rather, as Greek, "help them," namely, Euodia and Syntyche. "Co-operate with them" [Birks]; or as Alford, "Help in the work of their reconciliation." which laboured with me-- "inasmuch as they labored with me." Clement-- bishop of Rome shortly after the death of Peter and Paul. His Epistle from the Church of Rome to the Church of Corinth is extant. It makes no mention of the supremacy of the See of Peter. He was the most eminent of the apostolical fathers. Alford thinks that the Clement here was a Philippian, and not necessarily Clement, bishop of Rome. But Origen [Commentary, John 1:29] identifies the Clement here with the bishop of Rome. in the book of life-- the register-book of those whose "citizenship is in heaven" ( Lu 10:20 ; Php 3:20 ). Anciently, free cities had a roll book containing the names of all those having the right of citizenship (compare Ex 32:32 ; Psa 69:28 ; Eze 13:9 ; Da 12:1 ; Re 20:12 ; 21:27 ).

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17806"/><div sID="gen36132" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17806"/><hi type="bold">5. moderation--</hi>from a Greek root, "to yield," whence yieldingness [Trench]; or from a root, "it is fitting," whence "reasonableness of dealing" [Alford], that considerateness for others, not urging one's own rights to the uttermost, but waiving a part, and thereby rectifying the injustices of justice. The archetype of this grace is God, who presses not the strictness of His law against us as we deserve (<reference osisRef="Ps.130.3">Psa 130:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.130.4">4</reference>); though having exacted the fullest payment for us from our Divine Surety. There are included in "moderation," candor and kindliness. Joy in the Lord raises us above rigorism towards others (<reference osisRef="Phil.4.5">Php 4:5</reference>), and carefulness (<reference osisRef="Phil.4.6">Php 4:6</reference>) as to one's own affairs. Sadness produces morose harshness towards others, and a troublesome spirit in ourselves.<div eID="gen36132" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36133" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Let ... be known--</hi>that is, in your conduct to others, let nothing inconsistent with "moderation" be seen. Not a precept to make a display of moderation. Let this grace "be known" to men in acts; let "your requests be made to God" in word (<reference osisRef="Phil.4.6">Php 4:6</reference>).<div eID="gen36133" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36134" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unto all men--</hi>even to the "perverse" (<reference osisRef="Phil.2.15">Php 2:15</reference>), that so ye may win them. Exercise "forbearance" even to your persecutors. None is so ungracious as not to be kindly to someone, from some motive or another, on some occasion; the believer is to be so "unto all men" at all times.<div eID="gen36134" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36135" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">The Lord is at hand--</hi>The Lord's coming again speedily is the grand motive to every Christian grace (<reference osisRef="Jas.5.8">Jas 5:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jas.5.9">9</reference>). Harshness to others (the opposite of "moderation") would be taking into our own hands prematurely the prerogatives of judging, which belongs to the Lord alone (<reference osisRef="1Cor.4.5">1Co 4:5</reference>); and so provoking God to judge us by the strict letter of the law (<reference osisRef="Jas.2.12">Jas 2:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.13">13</reference>). <div eID="gen36135" type="x-p"/>

The archetype of this grace is God, who presses not the strictness of His law against us as we deserve ( Psa 130:3 , 4 ); though having exacted the fullest payment for us from our Divine Surety. entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17807"/><div sID="gen36136" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17807"/>6. Translate, "Be anxious about nothing." Care and prayer are as mutually opposed as fire and water [Bengel].<div eID="gen36136" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36137" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by prayer and supplication--</hi>Greek, "by the prayer and the supplication" appropriate to each case [Alford]. Prayer for blessings; and the general term. Supplication, to avert ills; a special term, suppliant entreaty (see on <reference osisRef="Eph.6.18">Ep 6:18</reference>).<div eID="gen36137" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36138" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thanksgiving--</hi>for every event, prosperity and affliction alike (<reference osisRef="1Thess.5.18">1Th 5:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.5.13">Jas 5:13</reference>). The Philippians might remember Paul's example at Philippi when in the innermost prison (<reference osisRef="Acts.16.25">Ac 16:25</reference>). Thanksgiving gives effect to prayer (<reference osisRef="2Chr.20.21">2Ch 20:21</reference>), and frees from anxious carefulness by making all God's dealings matter for praise, not merely for resignation, much less murmuring. "Peace" is the companion of "thanksgiving" (<reference osisRef="Phil.4.7">Php 4:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.3.15">Col 3:15</reference>).<div eID="gen36138" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36139" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">let your requests be made known unto God--</hi>with generous, filial, unreserved confidence; not keeping aught back, as too great, or else too small, to bring before God, though you might feel so as to your fellow men. So Jacob, when fearing Esau (<reference osisRef="Gen.32.9-Gen.32.12">Ge 32:9-12</reference>); Hezekiah fearing Sennacherib (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.14">2Ki 19:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.37.5">Psa 37:5</reference>). <div eID="gen36139" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 6. Translate, "Be anxious about nothing." Care and prayer are as mutually opposed as fire and water [Bengel]. by prayer and supplication-- Greek, "by the prayer and the supplication" appropriate to each case [Alford]. Prayer for blessings; and the general term. Supplication, to avert ills; a special term, suppliant entreaty (see on Ep 6:18 ). thanksgiving-- for every event, prosperity and affliction alike ( 1Th 5:18 ; Jas 5:13 ). The Philippians might remember Paul's example at Philippi when in the innermost prison ( Ac 16:25 ). Thanksgiving gives effect to prayer ( 2Ch 20:21 ), and frees from anxious carefulness by making all God's dealings matter for praise, not merely for resignation, much less murmuring. "Peace" is the companion of "thanksgiving" ( Php 4:7 ; Col 3:15 ). let your requests be made known unto God-- with generous, filial, unreserved confidence; not keeping aught back, as too great, or else too small, to bring before God, though you might feel so as to your fellow men. So Jacob, when fearing Esau ( Ge 32:9-12 ); Hezekiah fearing Sennacherib ( 2Ki 19:14 ; Psa 37:5 ).

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17808"/><div sID="gen36140" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17808"/><hi type="bold">7. And--</hi>The inseparable consequence of thus laying everything before God in "prayer with thanksgiving."<div eID="gen36140" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36141" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">peace--</hi>the dispeller of "anxious care" (<reference osisRef="Phil.4.6">Php 4:6</reference>).<div eID="gen36141" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36142" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of God--</hi>coming from God, and resting in God (<reference osisRef="John.14.27">Joh 14:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.16.33">16:33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.3.15">Col 3:15</reference>).<div eID="gen36142" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36143" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">passeth--</hi>surpasseth, or exceedeth, all man's notional powers of understanding its full blessedness (<reference osisRef="1Cor.2.9">1Co 2:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.10">10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.3.20">Ep 3:20</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Prov.3.17">Pr 3:17</reference>).<div eID="gen36143" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36144" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall keep--</hi>rather, "shall guard"; shall keep as a well-garrisoned stronghold (<reference osisRef="Isa.26.1">Is 26:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.26.3">3</reference>). The same Greek verb is used in <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.5">1Pe 1:5</reference>. There shall be peace secure within, whatever outward troubles may besiege.<div eID="gen36144" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36145" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hearts and minds--</hi>rather, "hearts (the seat of the thoughts) and thoughts" or purposes.<div eID="gen36145" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36146" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">through--</hi>rather as Greek, "in Christ Jesus." I am full-- Greek, "I am filled full." the odour of a sweet smell-- (See on Ep 5:2 ). The figure is drawn from the sweet-smelling incense which was burnt along with the sacrifices; their gift being in faith was not so much to Paul, as to God ( Mt 25:40 ), before whom it "came up for a memorial" ( Ac 10:4 ), sweet-smelling in God's presence ( Ge 8:21 ; Re 8:3 , 4 ). sacrifice acceptable-- ( He 13:16 ).
entries.reader_content_plain: 18. But-- Though "the gift" is not what I chiefly "seek after" ( Php 4:17 ), yet I am grateful for the gift, and hereby acknowledge it as ample for all my needs. Translate, "I have all" that I want, "and more than enough." Literally, as English Version, "I abound" over and above my needs. entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17823"/><div sID="gen36195" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17823"/><hi type="bold">22. they that are of Cæsar's household--</hi>the slaves and dependents of Nero who had been probably converted through Paul's teaching while he was a prisoner in the Prætorian barrack attached to the palace. Philippi was a Roman "colony," hence there might arise a tie between the citizens of the mother city and those of the colony; especially between those of both cities who were Christians, converted as many of them were by the same apostle, and under like circumstances, he having been imprisoned at Philippi, as he now is at Rome. <div eID="gen36195" type="x-p"/>
